title: Tiered Degradation Notification and Dashboard Flow
author: Riley Thompson
content:
Summary

This page defines the platform-wide approach to detect, visualize, and notify teams of progressive service degradation. The goal is to reduce noisy alerts, accelerate correct remediation, and provide a single source of truth (dashboards + notification matrix + runbook steps) for each degradation tier.

Why this exists

- High-level problem: our current alerts frequently trigger directly into P0 channels or are too noisy for meaningful action. Engineers either ignore noisy signals or are paged for transient, non-impactful spikes.
- This doc establishes: (1) explicit degradation tiers tied to SLOs and latency/cost signals, (2) dashboard patterns that surface actionable context, and (3) a notification and escalation matrix mapped to each tier and owner.

Audience

- Platform operators, SREs, service owners, oncall engineers, and dashboard owners.

Scope and definitions

- Service: any Redwood microservice, runtime component, or customer-facing inference endpoint.
- Degradation tier: ordered categories (INFO, T1, T2, T3) representing increasing impact.
- Primary SLI types: request_latency_95, request_errors_rate (5m), token_throughput, and kv_prefix_cache_hit_rate.
- Observable: any metric, trace, or log attribute that maps to an SLI.

Degradation tiers (short)

1) INFO (monitor): early indicators, no immediate paging. Show in dashboards and slack #platform-monitoring.
2) T1 (minor impact): noticeable SLO drift for a subset of customers; page only primary service owner during business hours.
3) T2 (major impact): cross-tenant latency/error regression; page oncall and platform-sre; begin mitigation playbook.
4) T3 (outage): service-level SLOs violated for >5m or critical downstream failing; full incident response (pager, status page, exec-notify).

SLO mapping and thresholds (examples)

| SLI | Normal threshold | T1 threshold | T2 threshold | T3 threshold |
|-----|------------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| request_latency_95 | < 200ms | 200–350ms | 350–800ms | > 800ms |
| request_errors_rate (5m) | < 0.5% | 0.5–1.5% | 1.5–5% | > 5% |
| token_throughput_utilization | < 70% | 70–85% | 85–95% | > 95% |
| kv_prefix_cache_hit_rate | > 90% | 80–90% | 60–80% | < 60% |

Design principles for dashboards

- Top-level deck per service: Health (SLOs + degradation tier), Latency distribution, Error classes, Dependency map, Recent deploys, Token/cost signals.
- Use tokenized SLIs (per-route or per-model) so we can attribute impact to expensive inference paths.
- Show both aggregated and sampled per-customer views (last 1h, 6h, 24h).
- Annotate graph with deploys and config changes (feature flags, quantization rollouts).
- Keep a compact incident summary panel at the top of the dashboard: current tier, active pages, playbook link, last update.

Alert rules (examples)

- Alert naming convention: <team>-<service>-<SLI>-<tier> (e.g. platform-runtime-kvcache-T2).
- Prefer Prometheus/Thanos expressions for enforcement; Datadog for composite/behavioral monitors.

Prometheus example (T2 latency):

ALERT PlatformServiceHighP95
  IF histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="runtime"}[5m])) by (le)) > 0.35
  FOR 5m
  LABELS {severity="page", tier="T2"}
  ANNOTATIONS {
    summary="runtime p95 > 350ms for 5m",
    runbook="/confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/runtime-latency-mitigation-runbook"
  }

Datadog composite example (T1 error spike):

- query A: avg(last_5m):sum:service.request_errors_rate{service:embedder} by {env} > 0.01
- query B: avg(last_5m):sum:service.request_volume{service:embedder} by {env} > 100
- composite: A AND B triggers (reduce noisy spikes from low-volume queues)

Notification matrix

| Tier | Who is notified | Channels | Escalation window | Visible dashboard panel |
|------|-----------------|----------|-------------------|------------------------|
| INFO | service-owner, platform-monitoring | #platform-monitoring (Slack), email digest | none | Health summary + SLI sparkline |
| T1 | service-owner | Slack (owner channel), email, PagerDuty (business hours only) | 30m -> owner escalates to platform-sre if unresolved | Service health + recent traces |
| T2 | oncall, platform-sre, service-owner | PagerDuty (all-hours), #incident-ops Slack, email | 15m -> full SRE engagement | Full deck + dependency map + token cost panel |
| T3 | Incident Commander, exec-runbook | PagerDuty critical, #incident-ops, status.redwood.com, Exec cadence | immediate -> P1 war room | Incident summary panel + public status link |

Runbook actions by tier (condensed)

T1 (owner):
1. Check dashboard SLI panels and last deploys.
2. Review trace samples for upstream errors or cold starts.
3. If error class matches known issue, apply hotfix or rollback change.
4. If no immediate fix, open incident ticket and mark as T1; update dashboard.

T2 (oncall + SRE):
1. Triage root cause using dependency map, sample traces, and KV cache metrics.
2. Apply mitigation: scale pool, enable fallback model variant, evict cold workers, or increase batching window.
3. Notify affected product teams and customers (if SLA impact).
4. Document timeline, actions, and telemetry in the incident ticket.

T3 (Incident Response):
1. Declare incident, assign Incident Commander and Scribe.
2. Run full incident checklist (paging, communications, privacy, legal if needed).
3. Execute emergency mitigations (traffic cutover, global fallback to hosted-compatible model variant).
4. Publish status and begin triage, followed by RCA within SLA windows.

Dashboard implementation checklist (owners must complete before an alert goes live)

- [ ] SLI definitions verified in SLI registry and linked to dashboard panels.
- [ ] Templated dashboard variables: environment, region, model, route, tenant.
- [ ] Top summary panel shows computed degradation tier (stringized) and most recent alert.
- [ ] Runbook link embedded with one-click to the service runbook.
- [ ] Annotated recent deploys (CI/CD metadata).
- [ ] Token-cost estimator panel for the last 24h and 7d.

Testing and rollout plan for new alerts

1. Create alerts in "monitoring-staging" and run for 48h to collect noise statistics.
2. Run a gameday where platform ops intentionally triggers each tier using synthetic traffic.
3. Adjust thresholds based on false positive/negative rates.
4. Roll out to production with "info-only" mode for 7 days, then enable T1 paging.

Ownership and maintenance

- Dashboard owner: primary service owner (should be in the service README).
- Alert owner: platform-sre for cross-service alerts; service owner for single-service alerts.
- Quarterly review: owners must review SLI thresholds and dependency annotations.
- On-call rotation: platform-sre leads on-call for T2/T3.

Retrospective triggers

- Any T2/T3 event will trigger a 1-week retro to identify dashboard/alert tuning opportunities.
- A periodic retrospective (quarterly) should review all INFO/T1 events to find recurring noise patterns.

Examples and sample queries

- Splunk/Logs: "service=runtime AND level=error | timechart span=1m count by error_class"
- Datadog graph query: avg:last_5m(request_latency{service:runtime,env:prod}) by {model} 
- Example tokenization SLI (pseudo-SQL):
  SELECT model, route, SUM(tokens_out) as tokens, PERCENTILE(latency_ms, 95) as p95 FROM telemetry.events WHERE env='prod' AND time > now() - interval '1 hour' GROUP BY model, route ORDER BY tokens DESC;

Appendix: sample incident annotation template (copy into incident ticket)

- Incident ID: 
- Start time: 
- Declared tier: 
- Initial SLI that triggered: 
- Immediate mitigation taken: 
- Owners paged: 
- Customer impact description: 
- Follow-up actions:

Open questions (to be reviewed during quarterly retro)

- Should we add per-customer severity weighting for enterprise tenants to trigger faster escalations?
- Do we need a separate tokenized SLI for embeddings-heavy customers vs chat-heavy routes?
